title: The chariot
hook: is the chariot the axle, the wheels, the pole? "Nagasena" is a name for parts together (Milinda, Book 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king's questions: Milinda meets Nagasena, and they agree to talk as scholars. This week the teaching took root. A bodhi tree cutting that still grows, a canon on palm leaves, stupas to walk around, an empty throne, a first face in stone, and a king with questions. Today, his first one. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

The king asks the simplest question there is: what's your name? And the monk gives an answer nobody at court expects. He's called Nagasena, he says. That's what his parents and his fellow monks call him. But it's only a name, a way of speaking. No lasting person is found behind it. The king turns to his courtiers, half amused, half offended. If there's no person here, he says, then who wears these robes? Who keeps the rules? Who gets the credit when someone gives alms, and who's to blame if someone harms you? Nagasena doesn't argue. He asks the king how he got here today.
screen: `WHAT'S YOUR NAME?` → `ONLY A NAME, A WAY OF SPEAKING.` → `THEN WHO WEARS THE ROBES?`

segments.voice: First, the chariot at the door. The king came by chariot, he says, not on foot. So Nagasena asks him to point to it. Is the pole the chariot? No. The axle? No. The wheels? No. The frame, the yoke, the reins? No, no, no. Then is the chariot all of these together? No. Something apart from them? No again. Second, the turn. Nagasena springs his own words back on him: then there is no chariot, and the king has told a falsehood in front of his whole court. The courtiers cheer for the monk. And the king, to his credit, works it out aloud. He hasn't lied, he says. Chariot is the name used for the pole, the axle, the wheels, the frame and the rest, when they come together. Third, the point. Just so, Nagasena says. Nagasena is the name used for this body, these feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness, when they come together. Nothing is hidden behind the parts; the name is real as a name. Then Nagasena recalls a verse spoken by a nun named Vajira in the older suttas: where the parts are gathered, people say chariot; where the parts of a life are present, people say a being. The king praises the answer. Fourth, what this does and doesn't say. It doesn't say Nagasena isn't there, or that names are lies. The king still rides home in his chariot. It says a name points to parts working together, not to a fixed core inside them. Buddhists call this anatta, not-self, and this simile is one of the ways teachers still explain it. A chariot gets you across town just fine. It just can't be found apart from its parts.
screen: `IS THE POLE THE CHARIOT? THE WHEELS?` · `THE KING WORKS IT OUT ALOUD.` · `NAGASENA: A NAME FOR PARTS TOGETHER.` · `THE CHARIOT STILL CARRIES HIM HOME.` · then, large: `A NAME FOR PARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one thing apart in your mind. Pick something near you: a cup, a chair, a phone. Name its parts, slowly. The handle. The rim. The base. Where, among those parts, is the cup itself? Then, gently, turn the same question toward your own name. A body breathing. Feelings coming and going. Thoughts. Notice what the name points to. No need to reach a conclusion. Just watch the parts working together, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The chariot. Nagasena's simile: neither the pole nor the wheels nor anything apart from them is the chariot, and chariot is a name for the parts together. Today's word.
Your line: a name for parts. Today, when you hear your own name, notice the parts it gathers up: a body, a mood, a thought. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the chariot simile from the Questions of King Milinda, together with the nun Vajira's verse, to explain not-self: a name is used for parts working together, with no fixed core behind them.

fork.setup: you're the king. you rode here by chariot, and the monk has made you deny that the pole, the wheels, and every other part is the chariot. what do you say?
options: fine, then there is no chariot.
the chariot is a hidden thing beyond the parts.
chariot is the name used for the parts together.
fork.reveal: the king works it out: he hasn't lied, because chariot is the name used when the parts come together. Nagasena says, just so with his own name.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: chariot. the simile Nagasena uses for his own name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle that proves nobody exists.
what it means: a name is real as a name, and it points to parts working together, not to a fixed core inside them.
what a scholar hears: Nagasena backs the simile with the nun Vajira's verse from the Samyutta Nikaya; the teaching is anatta, not-self.

notes: Parts listed (pole, axle, wheels, frame, yoke, reins) follow the Milindapanha list as I recall it; the text also includes items such as the banner-staff and goad. Confirm.
'This simile is one of the ways teachers still explain it': general statement about present-day teaching; confirm.
Week-end review (days 862–868) folded into the review segment.
'The courtiers cheer for the monk': in the text the Yonakas and monks applaud Nagasena; confirm.
